sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Multi-stage: golang image for build, minimal image for runtime. COPY go.mod go.sum → download deps → COPY source → CGO_ENABLED=0 go build → copy the binary to a scratch/alpine image. Final image is megabytes.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The multi-stage Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build (the golang image)
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Layer caching: go.mod/go.sum first (deps change rarely)
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download

COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o server .

# Stage 2: Runtime (minimal — just the binary)
FROM alpine:latest
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/server"]
```

Why multi-stage: the build stage (golang image — the toolchain, ~800MB) stays behind; the runtime stage copies ONLY the compiled binary (~15MB) into an Alpine image (~5MB) — the final image is ~20MB, not 800MB. Each stage is a separate image; only the final one ships.

The Go-specific flags:
CGO_ENABLED=0 — static binary (no libc dependency — runs on scratch)
GOOS=linux, GOARCH=amd64 (or arm64) — cross-compile for the target

The layer caching (the CI-speed win): COPY go.mod go.sum FIRST + RUN go mod download. The dependency layer only rebuilds when go.mod changes. Then COPY . . (the code — changes every build, but the cached dep layer survives). Without this, every build re-downloads the world.

The variants: scratch (FROM scratch — literally empty: the binary alone, 15MB, zero CVE surface); alpine (the convenience shell: ~5MB, the busybox tools); distroless (the hardened middle: no shell, no package manager, minimal).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S1[Stage 1: golang 1.22-alpine] --> M[COPY go.mod go.sum] --> DL[RUN go mod download — CACHED]
    M → S[COPY . .] --> B[CGO_ENABLED=0 go build]
    S2[Stage 2: alpine or scratch] --> CP[COPY --from=builder /app/server]
    CP --> CMD[CMD /server]
    B -->|only the binary| CP
    style S1 fill:#ff9
    style S2 fill:#9f9
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The static-binary mechanics: CGO_ENABLED=0 makes the Go compiler emit a binary with no cgo calls — no libc linkage. The binary is completely self-contained (the Go runtime, the net stack, everything linked in) — which is why FROM scratch works. With CGO (a SQLite driver, for instance), the binary needs the C library, and scratch fails — the Dockerfile needs alpine or distroless.

The build-cache internals: Docker layers are content-addressed — COPY go.mod go.sum + RUN go mod download form two layers; the second is valid until the first's content changes. COPY . . is the layer that invalidates every build (the source changes). The ordering — rarely-changing first (deps), frequently-changing last (code) — is the caching discipline for any language's Dockerfile.

The distroless-vs-alpine-vs-scratch trade: scratch (5MB with the binary — zero attack surface, nothing to debug with); alpine (a shell for debugging — but a bigger surface + musl libc nuances); distroless (Google's images: no shell, minimal but with certs/timezone — the production default). The choice: scratch/distroless for prod, alpine for the debuggability during development.
